Everything about getting registers into parquet and reading them with
[`fastreg`](https://dp-next.github.io/fastreg/), in the order most people need
it:

1. **[Point fastreg at your registers](#fastreg-paths)** - one `options()` call
   at the top of each script. Every `read_register()` example in this guide
   assumes you have done this. If a colleague already converted the registers,
   this is the only section you need.
2. **[Convert SAS files to Parquet](#convert-sas-to-parquet)** - when your
   project received `.sas7bdat` and nothing has been converted yet. Done once
   per register, usually by one person for the whole project.
3. **[When `read_register()` cannot find the
   register](#when-read-register-fails)** - reading parquet that is not in
   fastreg's layout.
4. **[Several registers on one DuckDB connection](#duckdb-views)** - for
   heavy work across the whole population, where everything has to stay in
   the database until the result is small.

Which file types you meet on the server, and what opens each one, is [Phase 4 -
File types and loading](file-formats.qmd).

## What is parquet, and why use it? {#what-is-parquet}

**Parquet** is a file format built for exactly the kind of work this guide
does: a large table, read many times, usually filtered down to a few columns
and a cohort's worth of rows. Unlike SAS (`.sas7bdat`) or `.rds`, which store
data row by row and load the whole file before you can use any of it, parquet
lets you open a *connection* and read only what you actually ask for.

Think of a supermarket. You can either buy the whole shop and sort through it
at home, or send a shopping list and only have what is on the list delivered.
A SAS or RDS file is buying the whole shop. Parquet is sending the list first
- `filter()`, `select()` - and only paying for delivery (`collect()`) once you
know exactly what you want. That is why a filtered, cohort-sized extract from
a register with tens of millions of rows can come back in seconds, without
ever loading the whole register into RAM. See [Phase 4 - File types and
loading](file-formats.qmd) for the mechanics behind this (lazy vs. full
loading).

This is why almost every register on DST is worth converting to parquet once
- the rest of this page shows how.

## Point fastreg at your registers {#fastreg-paths}

If someone else already converted the registers, you do not convert anything.
You tell fastreg where they are, **once per script**, and then read them by
name. Ask whoever set the project up for the exact paths:

```r
# Point fastreg at the converted registers - done once per script
library(fastreg)

options(
  fastreg.project_workdata_dir = "E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/cleaned-data/",
  fastreg.project_rawdata_dir = "E:/rawdata/[projectnumber]/"
)
```

After that, `read_register("bef")` works by name, with no conversion and no path
in each call.

**Set it once, at the top of the script, next to the `library()` calls.** Every
`read_register()` example in this guide assumes it has been set, and none of
them repeat it: two lines of someone else's project paths in every code block
would be noise, and it would suggest the call belongs next to each read rather
than once at the top.

Two things that otherwise cost you time:

- **Write `E:/` with the colon**: the DST server is Windows, also when you log
  in from a Mac. fastreg's own guide shows `E` without the colon, but only
  because the example writes to a temporary folder with `fs::path_temp()`.
- **The folder does not have to be the innermost one**: you can set the path to
  `cleaned-data/` even though it holds several subfolders (`parquet-registers/`,
  `parquet-external/`). `read_register()` searches further down for the register
  name.

## Convert SAS files to Parquet {#convert-sas-to-parquet}

Most projects on DST receive registers as SAS files (`.sas7bdat`). Before you
can use them with `open_dataset()` and lazy evaluation, they must be converted
to Parquet **once**. After that you use them exactly like any other register.

::: {.callout-important}
**Relevant for most projects.** If you are working on a project
where the registers have not already been converted to parquet, this step is
necessary before you can run extractions. Done once per register - after that
the normal extraction pattern applies.
:::

<details>
<summary>Why Parquet is worth it (SAS vs Parquet)</summary>

| | SAS (.sas7bdat) | Parquet |
|---|---|---|
| Read time (1M rows) | ~30–120 sec | ~1–3 sec |
| Disk space | Large | 50–75% smaller |
| Requires package | `haven` | `arrow` |
| Lazy evaluation | No - all into RAM | Yes - filter BEFORE collect |

</details>

### Recommended: convert with `fastreg`

The recommended tool is the [`fastreg`](https://dp-next.github.io/fastreg/)
package (dp-next, on CRAN). It converts SAS registers to Parquet (partitioned by
year) and lets you read them back by **name**.

::: {.callout-important}
**Use fastreg's own guide for the conversion code.** The exact commands are
documented - and kept up to date by the maintainers - in fastreg's [Getting
started vignette](https://dp-next.github.io/fastreg/articles/fastreg.html). We
link to the relevant section below instead of reproducing code that could drift
out of date. You install it once with `install.packages("fastreg")` and point it
at your raw-data and output folders as shown there.
:::

#### Convert a single file

If you only need to convert **one** SAS file, use fastreg's `convert()` function -
it writes a single register to Parquet. See the [Getting started
vignette](https://dp-next.github.io/fastreg/articles/fastreg.html) for the exact
call.

#### Convert many files at once

To convert a **whole workspace**, the fastreg team recommends its **`targets`
pipeline**: `use_template()` copies a ready-to-run pipeline that converts all
your registers in parallel - reproducibly, and re-runnable when a register is
updated. See [Converting multiple registers in
parallel](https://dp-next.github.io/fastreg/articles/fastreg.html#converting-multiple-registers-in-parallel).

<details>
<summary>If fastreg is not available on your project: convert manually with haven + arrow</summary>

If you cannot install fastreg, you can convert a single register yourself. This is essentially what fastreg does under the hood:

```r
library(haven)    # read SAS file
library(arrow)    # write Parquet
library(dplyr)    # %>%, rename_with()

sas_file  <- "E:/rawdata/[projectnumber]/rawdata/my_register.sas7bdat"
parq_path <- "E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/cleaned-data/parquet-registers/my_register/"

# 1. Read the SAS file into R
df <- read_sas(sas_file)            # reads the entire file into RAM - we call it "df", but you can use any name

# 2. Standardise column names
df <- df %>% rename_with(tolower)

# 3. Write as Parquet
dir.create(parq_path, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
write_parquet(df, file.path(parq_path, "my_register.parquet"))

# 4. Verify - open it lazily like any other register
open_dataset(parq_path) %>% glimpse()
```

This writes one flat file with no `year=` subfolders, so `read_register()`
cannot see it (see [below](#when-read-register-fails)). Open it with
`open_dataset(parq_path)` as in step 4, or with fastreg's
`read_parquet_dataset(parq_path)`.

::: {.callout-tip}
**Read only what you need.** Even before converting you can save RAM by limiting what is read in:

- `read_sas()` (`haven`) takes `col_select = c(pnr, alder, civst)` (pick columns), `n_max = 10000` (first rows only - good for testing) and `skip =`.
- `heaven::import_SAS()` (pre-installed on DST) is even more efficient for large files and can filter on values - e.g. `keep = c("pnr","atc")`, `where = "..."` (filter rows) or `obs = 1000`.

You can also convert to Parquet (or `.dta`) in **StatTransfer**, available on every server in the shared environment.
:::

</details>

## When `read_register()` cannot find the register {#when-read-register-fails}

This is the direct consequence of how the parquet was laid out, which is why it
sits on the same page as the conversion. `read_register()` can **only** read
registers that sit in fastreg's own format:

```
<register>/year=YYYY/part-XXX.parquet
```

That `year=` level is what produces the `year` column you filter on later. It is
a partition marker, not a DST variable and not a date - see [Phase 4 - reading a
register split by year](file-formats.qmd#year-column).

Both halves count: the `year=` subfolder and the `part-` filename. This is not a
bug but a deliberate choice. The function is built for data converted with
fastreg's `convert()`, and is not meant to guess every way parquet files might
otherwise be named. If the register is laid out differently - say as one flat
folder of parquet files, or with filenames without `part-` - `read_register()`
cannot see it, no matter how correctly you set the path.

In that case you use one of fastreg's two other reading functions:

  | Function                                    | You write                       | Used for                         |
  | ------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | -------------------------------- |
  | `read_register("name")`                     | the register **name**           | registers converted with fastreg |
  | `read_parquet_dataset("path/to/folder")`    | the **full path** to the folder | a folder of parquet files        |
  | `read_parquet_file("path/to/file.parquet")` | the **full path** to the file   | a single parquet file            |

All three hand you a **DuckDB table** (a lazy *duckplyr* data frame - its
`class()` starts with `"prudent_duckplyr_df"`), so the rest of your code is exactly the
same whichever one you use.

::: {.callout-important}
**`read_parquet_dataset()` does not use your `options()` path.** Only
`read_register()` looks names up under the folders you set. The two
`read_parquet_*()` functions need the **full path**, including any subfolders
below the folder you set. So if you set the path to `cleaned-data/`, you still
have to write the whole way down:
`"E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/cleaned-data/parquet-external/lmdb"`.
:::

```r
# Find the register when read_register() cannot look the name up
library(fastreg)
library(dplyr)

# 1. Which names does read_register() know? It lists the datasets it can find
#    under the paths you set with options() - always start here.
list_parquet_datasets()

# 2. If the register is not on the list, point at the folder with the full path
lmdb <- read_parquet_dataset(
  "E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/cleaned-data/parquet-external/lmdb"
)

# 3. If it is a single file rather than a folder, use read_parquet_file()
table <- read_parquet_file(
  "E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/cleaned-data/parquet-external/my_table.parquet"
)

# From there the code is the same as after read_register()
lmdb %>%
  rename_with(tolower) %>%
  filter(eksd >= as.Date("2010-01-01")) %>%
  select(pnr, atc, eksd) %>%
  collect()
```

## Several registers on one DuckDB connection {#duckdb-views}

`read_register()` is the right tool for most extractions in this guide: a
cohort-sized filter, a few columns, `collect()`. Some steps are different. They
work on **the whole Danish population** and join two large registers before
anything can be reduced, for example the income cutpoints in [Socioeconomic
variables](socioeconomic-variables.qmd#faik-income). For those, open the
registers yourself as **views on one plain DuckDB connection**:

```r
library(DBI) # dbConnect, dbExecute
library(duckdb) # the DuckDB database engine
library(dplyr)

# 1. Open an empty DuckDB database in memory
con <- dbConnect(duckdb())

# 2. Optional: cap how much RAM DuckDB may use (its default is 80% of the
#    machine) and give it a folder to spill to when it needs more. Without
#    these, a big query can fill the machine's memory; with them it slows
#    down instead. Use a folder in your own project.
dbExecute(con, "SET memory_limit = '8GB'")
dbExecute(con, "SET temp_directory = 'E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/duckdb_tmp'")

# 3. One view per register. A view stores no data - it is a saved query that
#    reads the parquet files when you use it.
#    **         = this folder and every subfolder
#    *.parquet  = every file ending in .parquet
#    hive_partitioning = true reads the year from folder names like year=2015/
dbExecute(con, "CREATE VIEW bef AS SELECT * FROM read_parquet(
  'E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/cleaned-data/parquet-registers/bef/**/*.parquet',
  hive_partitioning = true)")
dbExecute(con, "CREATE VIEW faik AS SELECT * FROM read_parquet(
  'E:/workdata/[projectnumber]/cleaned-data/parquet-registers/faik/**/*.parquet',
  hive_partitioning = true)")

# 4. Lazy dplyr tables - nothing is loaded into R yet
bef <- tbl(con, "bef") %>% rename_with(tolower)
faik <- tbl(con, "faik") %>% rename_with(tolower)

# ... filter(), left_join(), summarise() as usual, collect() at the end ...

# 5. When finished
dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```

Edit the paths to your own project. If a register sits in one flat folder with
no year subfolders, use `'.../faik/*.parquet'` and leave out
`hive_partitioning`.

**Why this, and not `read_register()`, for these steps:**

- **Nothing is computed in R behind your back.** `read_register()` hands you a
  `duckplyr` table. duckplyr uses the same DuckDB engine, but when it cannot
  translate a step it falls back to computing that step in R's memory instead,
  with no warning. fastreg opens registers as "thrifty", so for a large table
  that fallback stops with a materialization error rather than running in the
  database; for a smaller one the data quietly ends up in RAM. A `tbl()` on a plain DBI connection
  uses `dbplyr`, which only ever sends SQL to DuckDB, and `show_query()`
  shows you exactly what it sent.
- **Both registers on one connection.** A join runs inside the database only
  when both sides live on the same connection. Two tables opened separately
  either fail with an error asking for `copy = TRUE`, or have to be
  collected into R first, which is exactly what a whole-population step
  cannot afford.
- **Exact quantiles.** DuckDB computes `quantile()` exactly, interpolating
  the same way as R's default. Arrow datasets queried directly give
  *approximate* quantiles (up to about 1% off in testing, with a warning),
  which is not good enough for cutpoints.
- **It can spill to disk.** With `memory_limit` and `temp_directory` set,
  DuckDB writes intermediate results to disk instead of running out of RAM.

This pattern has been run on DST for the income cutpoints in [Socioeconomic
variables](socioeconomic-variables.qmd#faik-income) and for extractions from
LMDB.
